column2: Writing precise instructions a computer follows exactly, step by step. (Stage 01)
A named box you store a value in so you can use it later. (Stage 01)
A named, reusable chunk of instructions you can call with inputs and get an output back. (Stage 01)
A blueprint (class) for things that bundle data and behaviour together; an object is one thing made from the blueprint. (Stage 02)
A defined way for one program to ask another program to do something. A menu of things you're allowed to request. (Stage 06)
A server is a program that waits for requests; a client is the program that sends them. Your browser is a client; a website runs on a server. (Stage 06, 07)
A program whose whole job is storing data safely and finding it fast. (Stage 05)
The language you use to ask a relational database questions. (Stage 05)
A particular way of organising data in memory so certain operations are fast (lists, dictionaries, trees, graphs). (Stage 03)
A step-by-step recipe for solving a problem, e.g. for sorting or searching. (Stage 03)
A way to describe how the time (or memory) a piece of code needs grows as the input gets bigger. (Stage 03)
A structure that stores key → value pairs and finds any key almost instantly. (Stage 03)
A chain of items where each one points to the next. Cheap to insert/remove in the middle. (Stage 03)
Data organised like a family tree: one root, branches, leaves. Folders on your computer are a tree. (Stage 03)
Dots (nodes) connected by lines (edges). Cities and roads, people and friendships, tasks and their dependencies. (Stage 03)
Directed Acyclic Graph: a graph where connections have a direction and there are no loops. "Some tasks depend on other tasks, and you can't have a cycle." (Stage 03)
Putting the nodes of a DAG in an order where every task comes after the tasks it depends on. (Stage 03)
A small, fast place to keep copies of things you use often so you don't have to fetch them from the slow place again. (Stage 03, 10)
A cache that, when full, throws out the thing you used **L**east **R**ecently. A dictionary + a linked list. (Stage 03)
One independent sequence of instructions running inside a program. A program can have several running at once. (Stage 08, 09)
A running program, with its own memory. Threads live inside a process. (Stage 08)
Dealing with many things at once (taking turns quickly). (Stage 09)
Actually doing many things at the exact same time on different CPU cores. (Stage 09)
A bug where the result depends on which of two threads happens to get there first. (Stage 09)
A "one at a time, please" sign that a thread must hold before touching shared data. (Stage 09)
A lock that allows up to N holders at once. "Only 10 downloads at a time." (Stage 09)
Two threads each waiting for the other to release a lock. Neither ever moves. 💀 (Stage 09)
A way to write code that waits for slow things (network, disk) without blocking everything else. (Stage 09)
The language browsers and servers speak: a request goes out, a response comes back. (Stage 07)
The plumbing that gets bytes reliably from one computer to another over the internet. (Stage 07)
The phone book of the internet: turns `example.com` into an IP address. (Stage 07)
Encryption so nobody in between can read or tamper with the request. (Stage 07)
A common style for designing web APIs around URLs and HTTP verbs (GET, POST, …). (Stage 06)
A simple text format for sending structured data between programs. (Stage 06)
A lookup structure that makes finding rows fast, like the index at the back of a book. (Stage 05)
The balanced tree structure most database indexes are built on. (Stage 05, 12)
Combining rows from two tables based on a matching column. (Stage 05)
A group of database changes that either all happen or none happen. (Stage 05)
The four promises a good transaction makes: Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable. (Stage 05)
Write-Ahead Log: the database writes "what I'm about to do" to a log first, so it can recover after a crash. (Stage 12)
Multi-Version Concurrency Control: keep old versions of rows so readers don't have to wait for writers. (Stage 12)
A line of jobs waiting to be processed. Producers add, workers (consumers) take. (Stage 10)
A process whose job is to take items off a queue and do them. (Stage 10)
Where jobs go after they've failed too many times, so a human can look. (Stage 10)
Try again after a failure, waiting longer each time (and randomly — "jitter") so you don't hammer a struggling service. (Stage 10)
Doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Essential when retries can duplicate work. (Stage 10)
A time-limited claim on a job. If the worker dies, the lease expires and someone else can take the job. (Stage 10)
After N failures in a row, stop calling the failing thing for a while instead of failing slowly forever. (Stage 10)
Telling upstream "slow down, I'm full" instead of silently drowning. (Stage 10)
A machine that spreads incoming traffic across several servers. (Stage 11)
Splitting one big database across many machines by some key (e.g. users 0–999 here, 1000–1999 there). (Stage 11)
Keeping copies of data on several machines for safety and read speed. (Stage 11)
A trick for deciding which machine holds which key so that adding a machine only moves a little data. (Stage 11)
Something that says "you may make at most N requests per minute." (Stage 11)
Several computers working together as one system — and therefore able to partially fail. (Stage 12)
When the network splits, a system must choose between staying consistent and staying available. (Stage 12)
How a group of machines agree on one value (e.g. who's the leader) even when some of them fail. (Stage 12)
A majority. Many distributed decisions need a majority of machines to agree. (Stage 12)
Being able to tell what your system is doing from the outside: logs, metrics, traces. (Stage 13)
The response time that 99% of requests beat. Tells you how bad the slow tail is. (Stage 13)
A packaged-up program with everything it needs, so it runs the same everywhere. (Stage 13)
A system for running and managing lots of containers across many machines. (Stage 13)
Automatically testing (CI) and deploying (CD) code every time it changes. (Stage 13)
A tool that measures where a program spends its time. (Stage 13)
The list of functions currently in progress, innermost last: `main → foo → bar`. (Stage 08, 13)
A neural network is a giant pile of numbers (weights). Training adjusts them; inference uses them. (Stage 14)
Training: the model learns from data. Inference: the trained model answers a prompt. (Stage 14)
A chunk of text (roughly a word or part of a word) the model reads and writes one at a time. (Stage 15)
The neural-network design behind modern LLMs; attention lets each token look at the others. (Stage 15)
The maximum number of tokens the model can look at at once. (Stage 15)
A chip that does thousands of simple calculations at once; VRAM is its own memory, and it's always too small. (Stage 16)
Prefill: the model reads your whole prompt. Decode: it generates the answer one token at a time. (Stage 17)
Time To First Token (how long until the reply starts); Time Per Output Token (how fast it streams). (Stage 17)
Running several requests through the GPU together to keep it busy. (Stage 18)
Saved attention state for tokens already processed, so the model doesn't recompute it for every new token. Lives in VRAM. (Stage 18)
Managing KV-cache memory in fixed-size pages, like an operating system does, to avoid wasting VRAM. (Stage 18)
The part of a serving system that decides which requests run, when, on which GPU, batched with whom. (Stage 18)
Ways to split one model across several GPUs when it doesn't fit on one. (Stage 19)
A small model guesses several tokens; the big model checks them all at once. Faster when the guesses are good. (Stage 19)
Storing weights with fewer bits to save memory and go faster, at a small accuracy cost. (Stage 19)
